tagline: When M:M is wrong, what causes it, and how to fix it with shared dimensions

slides.title: Many-to-Many in Power BI
slides.body: Many-to-many (M:M) relationships occur when neither join key is unique on either side. Power BI supports M:M cardinality natively, but a direct M:M between two fact tables is a common modeling mistake that causes ambiguous filters and incorrect totals.
slides.keyPoint: M:M between a fact and a shared dimension is sometimes valid. Direct M:M between two fact tables is almost always an error — use shared dimension tables as the bridge instead.

slides.title: Anti-Pattern — Direct M:M Between Two Fact Tables
slides.caption: FactSales and FactBudget are directly related on CategoryID. Both sides have duplicate values — this is a genuine M:M.
slides.issue: Bidirectional M:M between fact tables means clicking a row in FactSales filters FactBudget — budget totals become context-dependent on sales data. Budget vs Actual comparisons become incorrect.

slides.title: Why Fact-to-Fact M:M Breaks Reports
bullets: Ambiguous filter path: a region selection in a FactSales visual propagates through the M:M to FactBudget — budget figures change based on sales context, which is usually wrong.
RLS exposure risk: bidirectional M:M allows security filters to propagate through both tables, potentially exposing restricted rows to unauthorized users.
DISTINCTCOUNT and aggregations become unreliable — filters crossing the M:M boundary can double-count or miscount values.
Performance: M:M joins prevent VertiPaq from building efficient join hash tables. Query performance degrades significantly on large tables.
The symptom: 'Budget vs Actual shows incorrect totals when any region or category is selected.'
slides.warning: Never directly relate two fact tables with M:M cardinality. Fact tables should only relate to dimension tables.

slides.title: Correct Pattern — Shared Dimension as Bridge
slides.caption: DimProductCategory sits between both fact tables. Each fact table has a separate 1:M relationship TO the shared dimension. The two fact tables never directly relate.
slides.filterNote: DimProductCategory independently filters both fact tables via separate 1:M relationships. Selecting a category filters Sales and Budget in parallel — not one through the other.

slides.title: PL-300 Exam Key Points — M:M Patterns
bullets: Shared dimension pattern: two fact tables relate to the same dimension via separate 1:M relationships — this is NOT M:M between facts, it is two independent 1:M joins.
Power BI's native M:M cardinality type is designed for composite model scenarios (e.g., DirectQuery + Import), not for fact-to-fact joins.
True M:M use case: users assigned to multiple security groups. Use a bridge table (UserGroupBridge) with UserID and GroupID as composite key.
Star schema rule: fact tables should never directly relate to each other. All joins flow through dimension tables.
Exam question: 'Budget vs Actual report shows incorrect totals when a product category is selected.' Root cause: direct M:M between FactBudget and FactSales with bidirectional filtering.
slides.keyPoint: Fix fact-to-fact M:M by identifying the shared business key and creating a dimension table on that key. Both fact tables then relate 1:M to that dimension.
